title: Frassati the Dominican
hookLine: Pier Giorgio was a lay Dominican

lines: A PHOTO ON A ROCK FACE.
A LAY DOMINICAN IN CLIMBING GEAR.
cards: An old black-and-white photograph. A young man in a hat and climbing gear, roped, leaning into a steep slope of rock. Across the bottom, in his own handwriting, a short Italian phrase: verso l'alto.
Toward the top. He was a student in Turin from a well-known family, who could have spent his life comfortably. Friends remembered him as loud, funny, a practical joker, quick to suggest a hike.
And quietly, he had joined yesterday's people. Pier Giorgio Frassati was a lay Dominican.

teach.b: You met Pier Giorgio back on day nine hundred sixteen, at his funeral; today, his Dominican side. When he made his promise as a lay Dominican, he took a new name in the order: Girolamo, Jerome. He kept his ordinary life.

He studied engineering, argued politics, went to Mass, and dragged his friends up mountains. But the Dominican three, pray, study, share, ran underneath all of it. The sharing is the part his own family didn't see.

teach.h: HE GAVE AWAY EVEN HIS FARE HOME.
teach.b: By his friends' accounts, he visited the poor of Turin, bringing food, paying for medicine, giving away what he had, sometimes even his fare home, so that he walked. He didn't announce it.
When he died young, after a sudden illness, the story told about his funeral is that the streets filled with poor people his parents had never met.
That is a lay preacher's sermon: preached without a pulpit, and heard only at the end. And the mountains weren't a break from faith.

teach.h: THE MOUNTAIN WAS PART OF THE PRAYER.
teach.b: They were part of it. The Psalms in the Douay-Rheims say: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me."
Climbing was a way of going toward God with your whole body, roped to a friend, step by step.
Verso l'alto. The Church holds him up as a model for young people, and his phrase has become a kind of motto: not a call to be grim or perfect, but to keep climbing, with friends, toward the summit.

how: Some young Catholics in parish and campus groups take Pier Giorgio Frassati as a patron, and some organize hikes and climbs under his motto, verso l'alto.

games.q: you're Pier Giorgio. you've just given your last coins to a family in need, and it's a long way home. what now?
o: skip the visits from now on.

practice: Lift your eyes to the highest thing you can see: a ceiling, a treetop, a hill out the window, and breathe there. Then bring to mind one friend you'd like to walk uphill with, and picture the two of you climbing together.
If you pray, lift your eyes to the mountains, as the psalm says.

wordCard.voice: Frassati the Dominican. Pier Giorgio, a student and climber in Turin who joined the lay Dominicans and served the poor so quietly his family found out at his funeral. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian: toward the top. Pier Giorgio's own words on a photograph of a climb.

carryVoice: Your line: verso l'alto. Toward the top, and never alone on the rope. Same time tomorrow.
